target: AG1's claim that a federal Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and help working people and students vote
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably remove the time constraint because it does not require private employers to close or give workers paid time off. Many retail, food service, and other hourly workers still work on federal holidays or must arrange unpaid leave, so the people most likely to face scheduling barriers may still face them, and low-income workers could be disadvantaged rather than helped.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would not meaningfully help because private employers can still operate on federal holidays
objection: Even if a holiday does not legally force every private employer to close, it still changes the schedule people actually live under: schools close, many businesses reduce staffing or shut down, and polling places can be run with holiday-available personnel. That broader practical effect means the holiday can reduce scheduling barriers beyond what the opponent suggests.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday creates enough normal daytime availability to solve the scheduling problem
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably create the daytime availability claimed, because many low-wage employers stay open and continue normal shifts. Workers may still have to vote mid-shift or lose wages, so the holiday does not eliminate the time constraint for the workers most likely to be harmed.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday leaves the scheduling problem intact because workers still need employer permission to vote
objection: The holiday can reduce scheduling barriers even without universal employer closure, because election officials can staff polling places on a holiday and voters can use newly available daytime hours before, after, or around shifts. The benefit does not depend entirely on employers voluntarily granting time off.

target: AG1's claim that staffed polling places and adjusted election logistics make a holiday sufficient to decouple voting from work schedules
objection: Even if polling places are staffed, the core constraint is whether workers are actually free during voting hours to travel, wait, and return. Many hourly workers still work holiday shifts, so access remains dependent on employer discretion and unpaid time off rather than being fully separated from work schedules.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday cannot meaningfully reduce work-schedule barriers, supported by the fact that private employers may stay open
objection: International practice suggests otherwise: 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays. If holiday or weekend elections did not meaningfully help ordinary voters, they would not be such a common approach in comparable democracies, so the U.S. holiday could genuinely reduce scheduling barriers.

target: AG1's reliance on international weekend/holiday elections as evidence the U.S. holiday will improve access
objection: The international comparison does not prove the same effect in the U.S. because federal law here does not require private employers to close or give paid time off. In a system where private employers can keep people working, a holiday can merely shift the burden from polling-hours-vs-workdays to polling-hours-vs-whether your employer gives time off, leaving the barrier largely intact.

target: AG2's assumption that work-schedule constraints are the only important barrier
objection: The holiday also helps by changing school routines and childcare logistics, especially for parents. When schools close, many school-based obligations and childcare arrangements disappear from the day, freeing up daytime hours and reducing dependence on employer permission.

target: AG1's claim that school closures would meaningfully solve childcare barriers
objection: Many low-income parents rely on childcare that is not tied to K-12 school schedules, such as daycare, Head Start, after-school programs, or relatives. Those arrangements may not close when schools do, so the holiday does not reliably create true daytime availability and leaves the core voting barrier in place.

target: AG1's overall argument that a national holiday is a reliable turnout reform
objection: Research suggests that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms. Because it does not mandate paid time off or directly remove work-based barriers, it is an inefficient and insufficient way to increase turnout, especially for low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is too narrow because only employer-paid time off would matter
objection: A holiday affects more than employer-paid leave: it closes schools, alters school-based childcare routines, and expands daytime availability for workers and students. Those changes can meaningfully reduce the practical scheduling barrier even without a legal mandate for paid time off.

target: AG1's claim that school closure would reliably free parents to vote
objection: School closure does not reliably create usable daytime availability because many parents depend on childcare arrangements that do not follow the school calendar, such as daycare or other caregivers. Parents may still need substitute care or unpaid time off, so the holiday does not consistently remove the barrier.

target: AG2's claim that the childcare effect is unreliable and too inconsistent to matter
objection: In many households, childcare does track the school calendar, especially through school-run or school-based programs. When Election Day becomes a holiday, those school-linked arrangements close or change, which can give enough parents a workable voting window to reduce the scheduling barrier meaningfully.

target: AG1's causal chain that school/childcare changes will reliably raise turnout
objection: Even if schools close and some childcare changes, that does not automatically increase turnout because the main barrier for many low-income workers is still needing paid time off or avoiding wage loss. The holiday eases one piece of the schedule but does not consistently remove the actual participation barrier.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday only changes a minor school-calendar detail while leaving core barriers untouched
objection: A holiday changes the whole weekday scheduling environment: school, childcare, and work routines all become easier to coordinate around voting. It also lets election administrators staff polling places and schedule voting around a holiday timetable, so the effect is broader than a minor calendar adjustment.

target: AG1's claim that school-closure and childcare disruption create new workable voting windows
objection: Private employers do not have to close or provide paid time off, and many hourly workplaces stay open on federal holidays. As a result, workers may still need to miss work without pay, so the holiday can rearrange logistics without solving the core constraint of being free during voting hours.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is not reliably effective and only changes school routines
objection: The holiday does more than alter school routines: it changes the practical coordination of work, school, and childcare that produces the time barrier in the first place. By shifting all of those routines together, it can make voting practically feasible without requiring every employer to provide paid leave.

target: AG1's overall assumption that a federal holiday meaningfully expands availability for parents and workers
objection: For many low- and moderate-income voters, childcare and work schedules remain constrained even when schools close. Retail, food service, and similar hourly jobs often still operate on federal holidays, and childcare may not close with schools, so the holiday leaves the core wage-loss-versus-voting tradeoff largely intact.

target: AG2's argument that the holiday only shifts logistics rather than easing the actual barrier
objection: A federal holiday targets the whole scheduling bottleneck, not just one piece of it. It changes school and childcare routines, alters workplace timing for many standard weekday jobs, and gives election officials a more workable day to run polling, so it can plausibly function as a broadly effective access reform.
